description:
Our project, aims to use official NASA lunar data to analyze landing-site conditions, sunlight availability, Earth communication windows, and potential mission power risks.

Our mission is to transform complex scientific data into accessible, practical tools that support research, learning, and the future of space exploration.
summary: LunarPath is a web-based decision-support tool for choosing lunar south pole landing sites. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a ridge a few hundred metres away can decide whether a lander has power and whether it can see Earth. LunarPath combines real NASA data — Sun and Earth directions from NASA/JPL Horizons and LRO laser-altimeter terrain (LOLA) — for eight reference sites from NASA's Lunar Surface Data Book. It shows, hour by hour and over 30 days, when each site has sunlight and Earth in view, what terrain blocks them, and whether an assumed lander's battery survives. Users set their own mission requirements, and LunarPath ranks the sites using transparent, documented rules with no hidden score, explaining the evidence behind every result. It is honest about uncertainty: it shows how results change within ±60 m and with panel height, flags an unrepresentative NASA reference point, and states its limits (Earth line of sight is not a radio link; the power model is not flight-certified).
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunarPath answers a practical mission question: which lunar south pole site best meets a mission's needs for sunlight and Earth visibility, and why?

• 3D Moon with 8 NASA reference sites (NASA Lunar Surface Data Book, Table A2-2) and Sun/Earth direction arrows; fly into real 5 m LOLA terrain.

• Time view: drag through 48 hours (5 dates in Nov 2026) and see whether each site has sunlight and Earth in view, with countdowns to sunrise/sunset and Earthrise/Earthset.

• Key Findings: 30 days (1 Nov – 1 Dec 2026), same method for every site — sunlight hours, longest darkness, Earth line of sight, and the effect of panel height (2 m vs 10 m).

• Mission planner: users set requirements (minimum sunlight, longest darkness, Earth visibility, battery and panels). Each requirement is checked as "meets", "does not meet" or "insufficient evidence", and the sites are ranked by documented rules (no weights, no score), with the reason for every step.

• Power and seven failure scenarios using an energy-balance model with user assumptions.

• One-click 17-section mission briefing (PDF/JSON/CSV) with data sources, risks, limitations and SHA-256 checksums of every NASA file.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation come from NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441, every 30 min) at each site's NASA coordinate. The terrain skyline is computed from NASA LRO LOLA 5 m site DEMs (PGDA product 78) plus the 240 m polar DEM out to 240 km, including lunar curvature. A target is visible when its centre is above the skyline.

SCIENTIFIC HONESTY AND VALIDATION

• Every coordinate was checked to sit at the centre of its NASA terrain tile.

• Shackleton Rim's official point lies on the crater's inner wall (31° slope), so it is shown but not ranked.

• Results were compared with NASA's 18.6-year illumination maps (PGDA 69) at all 8 sites: Earth visibility agrees closely; some sunlight differences on steep peaks remain unresolved and are documented.

• Position sensitivity (±60 m) is shown as a sensitivity range, not a confidence interval. Earth line of sight is not a radio link; the power model is not flight-certified; one month does not represent all seasons.

IMPACT

Mission planners, students and the public can explore real NASA data, test their own requirements, and see why a site is preferred and how certain that is.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Express (Node.js), Recharts, hosted on Vercel. 124 automated tests.

USE OF AI (SI)

Code, data-processing scripts, tests and documentation were developed with help from an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude), and reviewed and tested by the team. The demo video voiceover was generated with ElevenLabs (AI audio); this is labelled on screen and in the video metadata. All video footage is a real recording of the app. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
